common_name: Sunsatia Peach Nemesia (Fragrant Trailing Peach-Orange Nemesia)

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings after hardening off into fertile, well-drained soil; like its Sunsatia series siblings, Peach flowers most heavily in cool spring and fall weather and can stall during the hottest part of summer.

directions: Plant rooted starts in full sun to light afternoon shade in rich, well-drained soil, spacing them to allow the trailing stems to knit together within a few weeks. Sunsatia Peach carries a soft blend of peach and apricot tones across its small, snapdragon-like flowers, each lightly fragrant, on a mounding-trailing plant suited to hanging baskets and window boxes. Keep the root zone evenly moist, since the fine root system dries out quickly in containers, and feed lightly every other week to sustain bloom. Shear the plant back by about a third after the first heavy flush to encourage dense rebranching and a stronger autumn show.

common_name: Sunsatia Pineapple Nemesia (Fragrant Trailing Cream-Yellow Nemesia)

planting.note: Plant transplants into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun once frost danger has passed; this pale-flowered Sunsatia sibling bleaches out in the most intense summer sun, so afternoon shade helps hold its color in hot climates.

directions: Set transplants into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to part sun, giving afternoon shade where summers run hot. Sunsatia Pineapple bears abundant creamy yellow flowers with a sweet, fruity fragrance over a dense, trailing mound, making it a strong filler-spiller choice for mixed containers and baskets alongside bolder-colored companions. Water before the soil dries completely, since nemesia's fibrous roots have little drought reserve in a container, and deadhead or shear lightly through the season to keep new buds forming. Expect the heaviest bloom in cool spring and fall weather, with a possible lull during peak summer heat.

common_name: Sunsatia Plum Nemesia (Fragrant Trailing Purple-Magenta Nemesia)

planting.note: Plant transplants after hardening off into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; Sunsatia Plum's deeper color holds up better in summer heat than the paler shades in the series, though bloom still peaks in cooler weather.

directions: Grow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, keeping moisture consistent since the shallow, fibrous roots dry out quickly in hanging baskets and window boxes. Sunsatia Plum produces a rich wash of purple-magenta flowers with a sweet fragrance over trailing stems that cascade nicely over a container edge, reading noticeably darker and moodier than the pastel shades elsewhere in the series. Feed lightly on a regular schedule to sustain the long bloom period, and shear the plant back after the first major flush to renew branching and encourage a fresh round of flowers as the weather cools in fall.

common_name: Flirtation Orange Diascia (Compact Trailing Orange Twinspur)

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings once the soil has warmed slightly in spring; Flirtation Orange is a compact, well-branched twinspur best suited to cool shoulder-season display in containers and border edges.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, fast-draining soil in full sun, taking care to avoid soggy conditions that quickly rot diascia's fine root system. Flirtation Orange produces warm, saturated orange flowers in tight spikes over a low, mounding habit, giving a brighter and more compact alternative to the pastel coral and apricot twinspur cultivars already common in containers. Water in the morning so foliage dries by evening, since persistent humidity around the leaves invites fungal problems, and shear plants back lightly after the first flush to maintain a tidy mound and encourage repeat bloom into autumn.

common_name: Sun Chimes Coral Diascia (Large-Flowered Coral Twinspur)

planting.note: Plant out young starts once nighttime lows stay reliably above the mid-30s F; Sun Chimes Coral, like its burgundy sibling, is bred for larger individual blooms than most twinspur cultivars and performs best in mild spring and fall weather.

directions: Grow in well-drained, humus-rich soil with excellent air circulation, since diascia is prone to rot in soggy or stagnant conditions. Sun Chimes Coral bears oversized, clear coral-pink flowers in dense upright racemes over a low, spreading mound, carrying the larger bloom size of the Sun Chimes line into a brighter, warmer shade than its burgundy counterpart. Keep soil evenly moist but never waterlogged, and water at the base in the morning to keep foliage dry overnight. A light shearing after the first bloom flush renews branching and helps carry color into the cooler days of fall.

common_name: Lemon Symphony Osteospermum (Pale Yellow African Daisy with Purple Eye)

planting.note: Transplant into full sun after the last frost in well-drained soil; Lemon Symphony is one of the longer-established vegetative osteospermum selections widely used in university container trials for its uniform habit.

directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil, since waterlogged roots quickly lead to decline in container-grown osteospermum. Lemon Symphony opens soft, pale lemon-yellow daisy flowers centered on a dark purple eye ringed with a deeper gold band, a cool, two-toned combination that reads calmer than the brighter purples and pinks typical of the genus. The compact, free-branching mound needs little pinching to stay full, and deadheading spent blooms keeps the display tidy and encourages continued flowering through the cooler parts of the season. Like other osteospermums, flowering slows during peak summer heat and picks back up as temperatures moderate in fall.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

common_name: Berry White Osteospermum (White African Daisy with Purple Reverse)

planting.note: Transplant into full sun after the last frost in well-drained soil; Berry White's petals close at dusk and on overcast days, revealing the contrasting purple reverse until they reopen in sun.

directions: Grow in full sun in well-drained soil, watering deeply but allowing the surface to dry between waterings to avoid root and crown rot. Berry White shows crisp white petals with a dark blue-purple center by day, but the undersides of the petals are stained deep purple, so the flowers close into solid purple buds at dusk and on cloudy days, giving the plant a changeable, two-toned look over the course of a day. Remove faded flower heads regularly to prevent seed formation, which otherwise slows the production of new buds, and trim the mound lightly in midsummer if it begins to stretch or open up in the center.

common_name: BeeDance Painted Yellow Bidens (Semi-Double Golden Trailing Apache Beggarticks)

planting.note: Set out vegetatively propagated starts after all frost danger has passed and nights stay reliably above 50F; the open, semi-double flower form keeps pollen accessible to pollinators.

directions: Plant in a well-drained mix in full sun, letting the surface dry slightly between waterings since overly wet soil is the most common cause of poor flowering in bidens. BeeDance Painted Yellow carries the same semi-double, open-centered flower form as its red-orange sibling but in a clear golden yellow, keeping the central disc of pollen exposed and easy for bees to reach. The dense mounding-trailing habit fills a basket or window box quickly without pinching and is self-cleaning, so spent flowers drop cleanly without deadheading. Feed lightly on a monthly schedule to sustain bloom through the heat of summer into fall.

common_name: Campfire Fireburst Bidens (Bicolor Red-and-Gold Trailing Apache Beggarticks)

planting.note: Set out vegetatively propagated starts after all frost danger has passed; Campfire Fireburst is part of a Proven Winners bicolor bidens line bred for a strong flame-like color break between the ray and center of each flower.

directions: Grow in full sun in well-drained potting mix, allowing the top of the soil to dry before watering again, since bidens flowers poorly and is prone to root rot when kept constantly wet. Campfire Fireburst opens flame-toned flowers with glowing red-orange tips fading into a golden-yellow base and center, a vivid bicolor break that stands out sharply against the plant's finely cut, ferny foliage. The vigorous mounding-trailing habit spreads quickly to cover a basket or large container, and flowers are self-cleaning, dropping cleanly without deadheading. Shear lightly if growth becomes leggy by midsummer to renew branching and keep the display full through frost.

common_name: Million Bells Cherry Pink Calibrachoa (Suntory-Bred Trailing Cherry Pink Million Bells)
scientific_name: Calibrachoa x hybrida 'Million Bells Cherry Pink'

planting.note: Set out vegetatively propagated starts after all frost danger has passed; Cherry Pink is part of Suntory's original Million Bells line, the breeding program that gave the genus its common name.

directions: Plant in full sun to part sun in fast-draining, slightly acidic potting mix, and feed regularly with an acid-forming fertilizer since calibrachoa is prone to iron deficiency chlorosis in neutral or alkaline media. Cherry Pink produces a dense cover of small, bright cherry-pink, petunia-like flowers over a low, flat, far-trailing plant, giving an intense solid-color sweep that works well massed in window boxes or paired with contrasting colors in mixed containers. The tiny flowers are self-cleaning and bloom continuously from planting until hard frost without deadheading. Pinch stem tips at planting to encourage early branching, and keep the root zone evenly moist, since the shallow mix in most containers dries quickly in full sun.
sources: Suntory Flowers — Million Bells cultivar information
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Calibrachoa for Florida Container Gardens

common_name: Scopia Great White Bacopa (Vigorous Trailing White Bacopa)

planting.note: Transplant out after danger of frost has passed into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Scopia Great White is a Suntory-bred bacopa selected for larger flowers and more vigorous trailing growth than older seed-raised bacopa.

directions: Transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, giving afternoon shade in the hottest climates to prolong bloom. Scopia Great White covers its trailing stems in small, pure white, star-shaped flowers noticeably larger than those of older bacopa strains, on a vigorous habit that cascades quickly over the edge of a basket or container. Keep the soil consistently and evenly moist, since bacopa wilts and drops buds rapidly once it dries out, and feed on a regular schedule to sustain the heavy, continuous bloom typical of this series. It pairs well as a classic white spiller beneath taller, bolder-flowered thriller plants in mixed container designs.

common_name: Scopia Double Lavender Bacopa (Double-Flowered Lavender Trailing Bacopa)

planting.note: Transplant out after danger of frost has passed into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; the extra petal layers of Scopia Double Lavender give it a fuller, denser look than single-flowered bacopa.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, keeping moisture consistent since the shallow root system has little reserve against drying out. Scopia Double Lavender produces small, fully double, soft lavender-purple flowers that give the trailing stems a fuller, more textured look than the flat, single blooms of standard bacopa, while keeping the same fine-textured foliage and cascading habit. Feed regularly through the growing season to support the extra petal layers, and avoid letting the mix dry to wilting, which causes buds and open flowers to drop. It works well as a softly colored spiller paired with bolder pastel or jewel-toned companions in mixed containers.

common_name: Sapphire Lobelia (Classic Trailing White-Eyed Blue Lobelia)

planting.note: Start the very fine seed indoors well ahead of the last frost, pressing it onto the surface since it needs light to germinate; Sapphire is a long-established trailing lobelia strain grown for its distinctive white-eyed blue flowers.

directions: Start the fine seed indoors on the surface of moist mix without covering, then transplant after frost danger has passed into consistently moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun. Sapphire bears small, rich deep-blue flowers each marked with a crisp white eye at the throat, a contrast that reads more vividly than solid-blue trailing lobelia strains and shows up well cascading from a hanging basket or window box edge. Keep the soil evenly moist at all times, since the shallow, fibrous roots dry out and the plant wilts quickly in containers during hot weather. A light shearing after the first flush of bloom encourages fresh branching and a second wave of flowers as temperatures moderate.

common_name: Laguna Sky Blue Lobelia (Vegetative Trailing Sky Blue Lobelia)

planting.note: Set out vegetatively propagated starts after frost danger has passed; Laguna is a Proven Winners lobelia line bred from cuttings for earlier, more uniform flowering than seed-raised lobelia.

directions: Plant rooted starts into consistently moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun, avoiding the hottest afternoon exposure in warm climates. Laguna Sky Blue smothers its fine, trailing stems in abundant clear sky-blue flowers, blooming earlier in the season and more uniformly than older seed-grown lobelia strains since it is propagated entirely from cuttings. It cascades well over the edge of a hanging basket or mixed container, pairing nicely with white or silver-leaved companions. Keep the soil from drying out even briefly, since lobelia wilts and drops flowers quickly once stressed, and shear lightly if bloom slows during peak summer heat to encourage a fresh flush.

common_name: Regatta Rose Lobelia (Heat-Tolerant Trailing Rose-Pink Lobelia)

planting.note: Start the fine seed indoors well ahead of the last frost, pressing it onto the surface since it needs light to germinate; Regatta is a trailing lobelia series bred for improved landscape heat tolerance compared with older strains.

directions: Start seed indoors on the surface of a moist, fine germination mix, then transplant after frost danger has passed into evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun. Regatta Rose bears an abundance of small rose-pink flowers over trailing stems, part of a series selected for better performance in summer heat and humidity than many older trailing lobelia strains, making it a reliable choice for hanging baskets and window boxes through a long season. Keep the soil consistently moist, since the shallow root system offers little buffer against drying out in a container, and shear the plant back lightly if flowering pauses during the hottest weeks of summer to prompt a fresh flush of bloom.
